opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's matched it more closely than I would have dared to predict, though the timing played out a little differently than we expected.

When we started d-Matrix back in 2019, our thesis was pretty simple: training was going to get all the attention early on, but over time the real volume, the real economic value, would shift to inference. Once you train a model, you deploy it and run it billions of times. We believed that inference would eventually dwarf training as a workload, and that it had very different requirements. It's memory-bound, latency-sensitive, and cost-per-token really matters. So we bet on a memory-compute integration approach, digital in-memory compute, because we felt the bottleneck wasn't going to be raw FLOPs. It was going to be moving data between memory and compute.

What we didn't fully anticipate was exactly how inference would evolve. Back then we were thinking about transformers in a more general sense. Then generative AI exploded, and suddenly you had these large language models where the interaction is conversational. Now with agentic AI, it's not one query and one response. It's an agent reasoning, calling tools, generating chains of thought, talking to other agents, and doing that in loops. That multiplies the number of tokens you need to generate per task enormously, and it makes latency critical, because if every step in the chain is slow, the whole experience falls apart.

So the core of our vision, that inference would become the dominant workload and that memory bandwidth and latency would be the key constraints, has been validated. Agentic and interactive AI basically made the case even stronger than we originally framed it. The part we've had to adapt is the scale and speed. Things moved faster than anybody expected, the models got bigger, context windows got longer, and the demand for low-latency, high-throughput token generation went through the roof. That's pushed us to think hard about how we scale out, not just at the chip level but at the system and rack level, and how we work with the software ecosystem so customers can actually deploy this stuff easily.

So the direction was right. The intensity of it surprised all of us.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic AI can call tools and operate in loops, but does not say AI builds tools that improve its own capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes d-Matrix’s early vision as inference becoming dominant and memory bandwidth and latency becoming key constraints. It does not say that the vision extended toward machines acting on interactive exchanges.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's matched remarkably well, and I say that with some humility because when we started d-Matrix back in 2019, the word "agentic" wasn't in anybody's vocabulary. But the core thesis was there from day one.

The bet we made was that inference, not training, would eventually become the dominant workload, and that inference would be fundamentally different in character. Training is a batch problem. You throw enormous compute at it, you don't care much about latency, and you let it run for weeks. Inference, when it's serving real users in real time, is a latency problem and a memory problem. The bottleneck isn't raw FLOPs, it's how fast you can move weights and activations between memory and compute. That's why we went down the path of digital in-memory compute and built Corsair the way we did, with compute sitting right next to the memory rather than shuttling data back and forth across a bus.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how quickly the industry would move from single-shot inference, where a user types a prompt and gets one answer, to these multi-step, iterative workloads. An agent might make dozens or hundreds of model calls to complete a single task. It's reasoning, calling tools, checking its own work, going back. Every one of those steps is latency-sensitive, and the tokens per second per user becomes the metric that actually matters, not just aggregate throughput. That shift validated our architecture more than we expected, because the memory-bound nature of the problem gets more acute, not less, as you chain these calls together.

So I'd say the direction was right, but the velocity surprised us. We thought we had more time before interactive inference at scale became the defining problem. It turns out the market arrived faster than we did, which is a good problem to have if you've been building for it.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents making repeated model calls, using tools, and checking their work, but it does not say AI builds tools that improve its own capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says the early vision centered on inference and memory-bound latency. It presents tool-using agentic workloads as a later shift the company did not fully anticipate, not as part of d-Matrix’s early vision.

astra-6.text:
It’s very much aligned with the direction we envisioned: inference becoming an interactive process, where the system is responding, reasoning, and taking multiple steps. Agentic AI makes that especially important because a single user request can trigger a whole sequence of model calls. Each of those calls adds latency and cost.

That’s the challenge we set out to address with d-Matrix—making inference fast and efficient enough to support those experiences. I wouldn’t say we predicted every detail of how agents would develop, but the underlying need is very consistent with our original vision.

r001.rationale: The response discusses multi-step agent activity and model calls, but does not describe AI building tools that improve its own capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says d-Matrix envisioned interactive inference involving systems that respond, reason, and take multiple steps, and connects that direction to agentic AI.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s very much in line with the thesis we started with: inference would become a major computing challenge, and delivering it efficiently would require a different approach. What’s been striking is how quickly the workloads have become interactive. You’re no longer just submitting a request and waiting for a result—you’re having a conversation, or an agent is taking multiple steps to complete a task.

That makes latency and efficiency especially important. With an agent, one inference can lead to another, so delays accumulate. You need fast responses, but you also need an economic model that works as usage grows. That’s the opportunity we built d-Matrix around. The direction has matched our vision closely; the pace and the breadth of the applications have been the exciting part.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents taking multiple inference steps, but not AI building tools that improve its own capabilities.

r002.rationale: It connects d-Matrix’s vision to interactive workloads and describes agents acting through multiple steps to complete tasks.
